case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v V.B. and M.B.
text:
This is a case under Part III of the
Child and
Family Services Act
and is subject to subsections 45(8) of the
Act
.
This subsection and
subsection 85(3)
of the
Child and Family Services Act
,
which deals with the consequences of failure to comply with subsection 45(8),
read as follows:

45.
-(8) No person shall publish or make public information
that has the effect of identifying a child who is a witness at or a participant
in a hearing or the subject of a proceeding, or the child’s parent or foster
parent or a member of the child’s family.

85.
-(3) A person who contravenes subsection 45(8)
(publication of identifying information) or an order prohibiting publication
made under clause 45(7)(
c
) or subsection 45(9), and a director, officer
or employee of a corporation who authorizes, permits or concurs in such a
contravention by the corporation, is guilty of an offence and on conviction is
liable to a fine of not more than $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not
more than three years, or to both.

reasons

part I:
introduction and positions of the parties

[
1
]

The Respondents V.B. and M.B. are the mother and
father of nine children.  They have a longstanding history of involvement with
the Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton (“the CCAS”) and the Children’s
Aid Society of Hamilton (“the Society”) dating from October 1999. This thirty
one day trial of an Amended Status Review Application was the culmination of
those many years of child protection involvement.  The Respondent M.M.
(hereinafter referred to as “the grandmother”) is the paternal grandmother of
the children. The parents’ two eldest children, A.B. (a girl), born […], 1992,
and M.B. Jr. (a boy), born […], 1997 were not the subject of these
proceedings.  The two youngest children of the family, four year old twin girls
N.B. and S.B., born […], 2011, were named as subject children in the original Status
Review Application, but the case as it related to them was resolved on a
consent basis on October 6, 2014, when Pazaratz, J. made an order granting the
grandmother custody of them pursuant to
section 57.1
of the
Child and Family
Services Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c. C-11, as amended (the
“CFSA”
).  The
trial involved the parents’ five middle children (hereinafter referred to
collectively as “the subject children”), namely:

•

Their ten year old son S.A. P.-B., born […],
2005 (hereinafter referred to as “S.”);

•

Their nine year old daughter M.A. P.-B., born […],
2006 (hereinafter referred to as “M.”);

•

Their eight year old daughter S.M. P.-B., born .[…],
2007 (hereinafter referred to as “Sh.”);

•

Their seven year old daughter V.M. P.-B., born […],
2008 (hereinafter referred to as “V. Jr.”);   and

•

Their five year old son A.J.T. P.-B., born […],
2009 (hereinafter referred to as “A.”).

[
2
]

The Society issued its original Status Review
Application respecting the subject children on March 7, 2014, requesting an
order for Crown wardship with access respecting  M., and an order providing
for  S., Sh., V. Jr. and A. to remain in the care of their mother V.B. subject
to Society supervision for six months.  It filed an Amended Status Review
Application on April 9, 2014, requesting an order for Crown wardship with
access to the parents respecting S. and M., and Crown wardship without access
respecting Sh., V. Jr. and A.  At the commencement of trial, the Society
advised that it was pursuing an order for Crown wardship with access to both
parents respecting all of the five subject children.

[
3
]

The grandmother was named as a party to the
Status Review Application because the children N.B. and S.B. were included in
that application, and those children were in her care pursuant to a final
supervision order dated October 23, 2013.  She filed an Answer and Plan of Care
in response to the Status Review Application in which she included a claim for
access to the subject children every Saturday at her home.  She attended at the
commencement of this trial and received assistance from Ms. Bingham, who
appeared as her agent only.  Ms. Bingham confirmed that the grandmother was not
presenting a plan for any of the subject children, and that she was not
pursuing any claims for court-ordered access to the children.  She indicated
that the grandmother would be testifying on behalf of the father M.B. during the
trial, but that she did not wish to participate as a party.  Accordingly, on
January 20, 2015, I made an order on consent of all parties and counsel for the
children removing M.M. as a party.

[
4
]

The mother’s counsel, Mr. Walkling, appeared on
behalf of the mother at the commencement of the trial.  He advised that as a
result of recent developments in the case, the mother had decided to consent to
an order for Crown wardship with access respecting the five children.   Mr.
Walkling emphasized that V.B.’s original goal was to have the children returned
to her care, but that V.B. had chosen not to participate in the trial because
she did not believe that the evidence would support her plan.   Mr. Walkling
and the Society presented me with Minutes of Settlement which the Society,
counsel for the children and the mother had executed, providing for an order
for Crown wardship with access regarding S., M., Sh., V. Jr. and A.  Those
Minutes of Settlement were marked as Exhibit 1 in the trial.  With respect to
access, the Minutes of Settlement provide for the mother to have access in the
discretion of the Society and supervised in the Society’s discretion.  They
further stipulate that access will occur at minimum twice per month for four
hours on each occasion if the Society agrees to allow the grandmother to
supervise access and the grandmother can accommodate visits of this duration
and frequency.  The Minutes of Settlement also provide for sibling access, in
the discretion of the Society and supervised in the Society’s discretion.
Specifically, they stipulate that the five subject children shall have access
with each other at minimum twice per month, as well as access with their
younger twin sisters N.B. and S.B. at minimum once per month.

[
5
]

Although the mother signed the Minutes of
Settlement described above, Mr. Walkling indicated that she would also support
an order placing the subject children with the father M.B. if the court
concluded after hearing all of the evidence that such an order was
appropriate.  He relayed that if such an order were made, V.B.’s position
respecting her access would be that access should be in the father’s and/or the
Society’s discretion.  Mr. Walkling stated that the mother had decided not to
participate as a party at trial, and had instructed him not to appear as
counsel on her behalf.   He stated that V.B. may testify as a witness on behalf
of the father.  The mother was in fact called as a witness for M.B.  Mr.
Walkling confirmed that V.B. understood that the court was not bound by the
terms which she, the Society and counsel for the children had agreed upon in
the Minutes of Settlement, and that the issues of placement and access would be
determined by the court based on all of the evidence adduced at trial.  On the
basis of these submissions, I excused Mr. Walkling from participating further
in the trial.

[
6
]

Ms. Bale is counsel for the children M., Sh., V.
Jr., and A., and Mr. Charko is counsel for the child S.  Both counsel appeared
at the outset of trial.  However, they advised me that their position in this
matter was the same, and that they had therefore received directions from the
Office of the Children’s Lawyer to request that Ms. Bale act as Mr. Charko’s
agent for the purposes of the trial.  I allowed this request and excused Mr.
Charko from participating further in the trial proceedings.  Ms. Bale and Mr.
Charko both executed the Minutes of Settlement described above which the
Society and the mother signed.  In her Closing Submissions, however, Ms. Bale
indicated that the evidence adduced at trial supported an order requiring that
all access between the children and both parents, as well as all sibling access,
be supervised unless otherwise ordered by the court in a subsequent proceeding.

[
7
]

The father seeks an order placing S., M. Sh., V.
Jr. and A. in his care and custody pursuant to
section 57.1
of the
CFSA
.
In
the alternative, he seeks an order placing the children with him subject to a
six month supervision order.   In the event that the children are made Crown wards,
his position is that he should have liberal and generous unsupervised access to
them, commencing with at least two visits per month for four hours on each
occasion.  With respect to the child A., the father enjoyed individual weekly
visits with him during the months leading up to the trial, until all access was
suspended in January 2015 because of another child protection investigation.  The
father seeks a specific access clause providing for this weekly one-on-one
access with A. to continue, one evening during the week from after school until
7:00 p.m.  The father supports the position of the Society, the mother and
counsel for the children respecting ongoing access between the five children
involved in these proceedings and between those children and the youngest
children N.B and S.B.

[
8
]

The issues to be decided in this case are as
follows:

a)

Do the children S., M., Sh., V. Jr. and A.
require ongoing protection through a court order dealing with placement and
access to them?

b)

If a court order is required for the ongoing
protection of the children, is it in their best interests to be made Crown wards,
or is an order placing them with their father M.B. in their best interests?

c)

In the event that the children are placed in the
custody of the father, is it in their best interests for the court to grant the
father custody pursuant to
section 57.1
of the
CFSA
,
or should the
placement be in the nature of a supervision order which would require the
Society to monitor the placement?  Furthermore, if the children are placed with
the father, would it be in their best interests to have access to the mother,
and if so, what terms of access should be ordered?

d)

If the children are made Crown wards, should an
order for access issue in favour of V.B. and M.B.?  In this regard, have V.B.
and M.B. met the onus on them of establishing that their relationships with the
children are meaningful and beneficial to the children, and that access will
not impair the children’s future opportunities for adoption?

e)

Is it in the best interests of the children to
grant an order for ongoing sibling access?

[
9
]

For the reasons set out below, I have concluded
that the children S., M., Sh., V. Jr. and A. continue to require protection
through a court order dealing with their placement and access issues I have also
determined that it is in the children’s best interests that they be made Crown wards
and remain in the care of the Society. I am satisfied that the relationships
between the parents and the subject children are meaningful and beneficial to the
children, and that an access order will not impair the children’s future opportunities
for adoption.  Accordingly, I am making an order for access to V.B. and M.B.
However, based on the seriousness and longstanding nature of the protection
concerns in this case, I am ordering that any access between the children and M.B.
and V.B. be supervised by the Society only, at least once per month but no more
than twice monthly, and that the other specifics of such supervised access be
in the discretion of the Society.  I agree with the parties that an order
providing for ongoing access between the siblings is in the best interests of
the children. However, given the serious concerns regarding the children’s
sexualized behaviours, which I will review in further detail in these Reasons,
I have ordered that all sibling access be supervised by either the Society or a
person approved in advance by the Society.

PART II:  CREDIBILITY AND RELIABILITY ASSESSMENT

[
10
]

The Society called eleven child protection
workers as witnesses in this trial.  They also called Dr. Kathleen McDermott,
who completed a parenting capacity assessment respecting the parents, Dr. Benjamin
Klein, who carried out a developmental assessment of the child A. and a
consultation respecting V. Jr., the child M.’s foster mother C.G. and Daniela
Lisi, a Clinical Therapist employed by Child and Adolescent Services.

[
11
]

The parents both testified at trial, and the
father also called the grandmother, Society Parent Support Worker Sandra
Phillips and his partner J.C. as witnesses.  The evidence of the father and his
witnesses conflicted in certain material respects from that of some of the
Society’s witnesses.  In addition, although M.B. called the mother V.B. as a
witness, their evidence was inconsistent on many important points.  Assessment
of credibility and reliability was therefore a very important component of my
deliberations in this case.

[
12
]

Counsel for M.B. did not in her Closing
Submissions highlight any particular concerns respecting the credibility of the
following witnesses who testified on behalf of the Society:

a)

Kim Colangelo;

b)

Julia Abell;

c)

Tory Baker-Reed;

d)

Janice Kinrade;

e)

Christine Conley;

f)

Jessica MacKenzie;

g)

Jennifer Johnston;

h)

Ashley Guimaraes; and

i)

Daniela Lisi.

[
13
]

I did not have any concerns regarding the
credibility or reliability of any of these Society witnesses.  They all
presented their evidence in a competent, organized and professional manner.
They had a reasonable recollection of their involvement with this family and
readily acknowledged if they could not recall specific details or events.   Their
evidence was not undermined in any significant way on cross examination.  Some
additional comments respecting Julia Abell are warranted.  Ms. Abell was the
CCAS Family Services worker involved with the family from October 2010 until
October 2011.  She was unable to answer a number of questions put to her on
cross examination because of her inability to recall.  However, I am satisfied
that her recollection respecting significant events and issues was very good.
Given the passage of time and the complexity of this case, her inability to
remember some details and events was not surprising or concerning in terms of
her overall credibility and reliability.

[
14
]

Andrea James was the Family Services worker
involved with this family from November 2011 until July 2014.  There were some
important discrepancies between her evidence and that of the father M.B., his
partner J.C., and the mother V.B.  These include the following:

a)

M.B. testified that when the file was
transferred from the CCAS to the Society in the fall of 2011, Ms. James told
him that he should only talk to her about any issues relating to his case or
the children, and that he was not permitted to speak to the Children’s Services
workers.  Ms. James denies having made any such comments to the father.

b)

M.B. alleged that Ms. James told him during a
meeting at the grandmother’s home that there were no concerns about him
regarding abuse or neglect of the children.  Ms. James testified that she had
no recollection of ever having made this statement, and that it did not sound
like something she would have said to the father based on the history of concerns
respecting his parenting.

c)

M.B. testified that he relayed concerns to Ms.
James that M.B. Jr.’s foster mother bought him cigarettes and allowed the boys
in the home to smoke marijuana.  Ms. James denied having ever received a report
from M.B. respecting these concerns.

d)

M.B. testified that he had a meeting with Ms.
James during which he relayed his concerns about certain aspects of the Parenting
Capacity Assessment and asked if the assessment of him could be re-done.
According to M.B., Ms. James stated that the Parenting Capacity Assessment could
not be repeated because of cost issues.  Ms. James denies having ever had this
conversation with M.B.

e)

M.B. and his partner J.C. alleged that Ms. James
spoke to J.C. by telephone in late August or early September 2013 and authorized
J.C. to be present during the father’s visits with the children.  Ms. James
denied that this conversation occurred, and testified that she never gave such
authorization and in fact never spoke with J.C.

f)

M.B. alleged that he asked Ms. James to
summarize the Society’s concerns about the children’s sexualized behaviours in
writing, but that Ms. James told him that she could not do that.  Ms. James
stated that the mother made this request of her and that she did write the
mother a letter dated March 22, 2013 in which she reviewed some of the
Society’s concerns.  She denied that the father ever made any such request.

g)

M.B. stated that Ms. James represented to him
that the child A. would be integrated into his care, and that his older brother
S. would follow a month later.  Ms. James adamantly denied having ever made any
such representations to the father.

h)

M.B. stated that Ms. James had told him that the
child A.’s original foster home had been shut down due to concerns about abuse
by the foster parents in that home.  Ms. James denied having made this
statement.  She testified that to her knowledge, the child A. was removed from his
first foster home after he suffered a mark to his hand, but there was never any
verification of abuse by either foster parent.

i)

M.B. alleged that Ms. James told him that there
were no verified concerns regarding sexualized behaviours by the children, but
merely allegations.  Ms. James denied having made this statement.

j)

V.B. testified that when the children were
reintegrated back into her care in the fall of 2013, Ms. James told her that
she should give the children the run of the house and not confine them to
specific areas.  Ms. James was adamant that she never gave any such direction,
and testified that in fact, she told V.B. to keep the children under her watch
at all times and not allow them to go to other levels of the home unless she
was with them.

k)

M.B. testified that after the completion of the
parenting capacity assessment by Dr. McDermott, Ms. James told him that Dr.
McDermott had urged the Society to carry out a “sneak attack” on M.’s foster
home to remove M. from the home due to concerns regarding the foster mother C.G.
Ms. James denies that Dr. McDermott ever made such a recommendation or that she
made these comments to M.B.

[
15
]

I accept Ms. James’s evidence over that of M.B.
and V.B.  Ms. James had a very sound recollection of events, and she presented
her evidence in a coherent and organized manner.   While she lacked
recollection on some points, this did not impact my overall assessment of her
credibility given the passage of time and the fact that the points in question
were not overly significant to the case.  Her evidence was not undermined
during cross-examination.  Furthermore, there is documentary corroboration
regarding her evidence on some of the above-noted issues.  For instance, there
is a letter from her to V.B. dated February 26, 2014 in which she indicates
that she clearly told the mother on more than one occasion that the children
needed to be strictly supervised while in her care.  With respect to the
suggestion that she authorized the father’s partner J.C. to attend the father’s
visits in August or September 2013, her case-note regarding her meeting with
the father on June 26, 2014 clearly indicates that she had never met or spoken
with J.C. up until that point, and that she would need to meet J.C. before
approving her attendance at visits.  My preference for Ms. James’ evidence over
that of the parents is also based on my overall concerns regarding the
credibility of both parents, which I discuss in further depth below.

[
16
]

The evidence of Society Family Services Worker
Jessica Hall conflicted in one material respect with that of the father, his
partner J.C. and Society Parent Support Worker Sandra Phillips.  Ms. Hall
testified that she told M.B., J.C. and Ms. Phillips that J.C. was expected to
attend visits in the father’s home with the child A. and to work with Ms. Phillips
so that the Society could assess her as a support person for M.B.  The father, J.C.
and Ms. Phillips denied that Ms. Hall had advised them of this expectation.
This issue was important because J.C. did not attend the sessions with Ms.
Phillips in the home.   I accept the evidence of M.B., J.C. and Ms. Phillips
over that of Ms. Hall on this issue.    Ms. Hall stated that she relayed this
expectation to the father and J.C. on October 7, 2014.  However, there is no
reference to this information in the portion of her affidavit relating to the
meeting that occurred on that date.  Despite this problem with Ms. Hall’s
evidence, I find that overall, she presented as highly credible and reliable.
She generally had a very sound recollection of events, and her evidence was not
undermined in any other significant way.  She was fair and even handed in
giving her testimony, and had many positives to say regarding both parents.
Overall, she was an extremely impressive witness.

[
17
]

The Society also called Dr. Benjamin Klein as a
witness to testify regarding his involvement with the children V. Jr. and A.
Dr. Klein was qualified as an expert in the area of developmental pediatrics,
for the purpose of giving opinion evidence respecting the development of
children.  He presented as an extremely knowledgeable, competent and articulate
professional.  His testimony was not undermined in any way during cross
examination.  He was a very credible and reliable witness.

[
18
]

The father M.B. suggested that there were
concerns regarding the credibility and reliability of the parenting capacity
assessor, Dr. McDermott, and the integrity of her report.  The concerns which
he raised were as follows:

a)

That Dr. McDermott did not make any reference in
her report to services which would be recommended for the father;

b)

That Dr. McDermott did not take the necessary
steps to inform M.B. about the assessment process and the importance of the
assessment;

c)

That M.B. needed his glasses to read during the
assessment and did not have them;

d)

That M.B. had been awake most of the night prior
to his interviews and testing due to work commitments, and this could have
impacted his performance;  and

e)

That most of the documents which Dr. McDermott
reviewed were from the Society, and she did not receive any materials from the
father.

[
19
]

I did not have concerns regarding Dr.
McDermott’s credibility and reliability, her methodology in carrying out the
assessment process or the integrity of her parenting capacity assessment in
general.  I am satisfied based on her evidence that she took appropriate
measures to ensure that the assessment process was carried out in a fair and
appropriate manner.  She addressed any concerns about M.B.’s challenges with
reading by personally reading all of the items of the inventories aloud to him
and giving him an opportunity to ask questions about their meaning.  M.B. did
not mention that he did not have the proper glasses.  Dr. McDermott was
satisfied that she obtained all relevant information from M.B. based on her
interviews.  M.B. did not at any point during the assessment process express
that he felt he needed more time with Dr. McDermott to tell his story.  Dr.
McDermott testified that M.B. did not at any point express concerns to her
about having not had sufficient sleep the night prior to his interview.  In
fact, based on the information which M.B. had provided to Dr. McDermott, I find
that M.B. had been fired from his employment shortly before the testing was
undertaken, and accordingly M.B.’s explanation for being tired was suspect.  In
any event, Dr. McDermott emphasized that she would have rescheduled the
appointment if she had had concerns that M.B. was not up to taking the testing
or carrying out the interview, and noted that she had done so many times in the
past in the context of other parenting capacity assessments.  Dr. McDermott did
not have any concerns during the process that M.B. did not understand the assessment
process, although she did have some concern as to whether he appreciated the
significance of it.   She noted that neither parent provided her with any
materials to review, and that she gave both parents an opportunity to respond
to any concerns which the Society had outlined in its materials.  She explained
that she did not refer to any recommended services for the father because M.B.
was not presenting a plan to care for the children at that point, and in any
event, she had concluded that he did not have the capacity to parent.

[
20
]

The Society also called the child M.’s foster
mother, C.G., as a witness.  C.G. has been M.’s foster mother since October
2011.  As I will discuss in further detail below, C.G. testified at length
about the many aggressive and sexualized behaviours which M. has exhibited
since arriving at her home, and many comments which M. has made about her
family.  Both M.B. and V.B. have raised numerous concerns about C.G., both
prior to and during the trial.  They alleged that C.G. has influenced M.
against her family, has conjured up concerns about sexualized behaviours, has
influenced M. to make false disclosures about her family members, and has met
with the foster parents of the other children in an attempt to influence the
other children as well.  The mother V.B. went so far as to suggest during her
testimony at trial that C.G. may have been the person responsible for M.’s
inappropriate sexual conduct.  The parents further alleged that Dr. McDermott
and Family Services Worker Ms. James had serious concerns about C.G.  Both
parents were of the view that I should accord very little weight to C.G.’s
evidence.

[
21
]

I do not agree with any of the concerns which
M.B. and V.B. raised about C.G.  As I have already noted, I accept Ms. James’
evidence that she did not have any concerns regarding C.G. as a foster mother.
Dr. McDermott indicated in her testimony that she had some concerns about the
intensity of the bond between C.G. and M., and the fact that M. was only
exhibiting sexualized behaviours in her foster home.  However, she acknowledged
that the latter concern would be alleviated if there was evidence of sexualized
behaviours by the other children after S. and M. were removed from their
original foster home.  As I will address in further detail below, there were in
fact sexualized behaviours by the other children after that time.   There was
no compelling evidence to support the suggestions that C.G. has tried to
influence M. and the other children against their family, or that she has
conjured up false allegations.  Although M. has made comments comparing her
foster home to her family home, and the two neighbourhoods where the homes are
located, I am not satisfied that these comments were in any way attributable to
inappropriate commentary or influence by C.G.  With respect to the fact that M.
has only exhibited sexualized behaviours in the foster home, the sexual abuse
therapist involved with M., Ms. Daniela Lisi, explained that it is not unusual at
all for a child to exhibit sexualized behaviours only in the environment where
they feel most safe and secure.

[
22
]

C.G. presented as organized, coherent, even
handed, genuine and comfortable in giving her evidence.  Her oral evidence was
consistent with information which Society staff documented that they had
received from her.  She provided very detailed information regarding M., her
challenges, and her progress. Her evidence was not undermined in cross
examination.  In short, I found her to be extremely credible and reliable.  She
impressed me as a truly remarkable woman.  I feel compelled to recognize her in
these Reasons because she has been subjected to considerable criticism by the
parents, with the result that M.S.’s placement with her has been carefully
reviewed and scrutinized by the Society.  I find that C.G. has endured many
challenges with M. since the child has been in her care.  M. has exhibited
extremely disturbing sexualized behaviours, aggression, anger, anxiety,
frustration, fear and sadness.  In short, the ride with M. has been nothing
short of an intense rollercoaster for C.G.  Notwithstanding these challenges,
C.G. has steadfastly stood by M., loved her dearly, and been a fearless
advocate for her needs.  She has been one of the most consistent people in M.’s
life since October 2011, as there have been numerous changes in Society Family
Services Workers and Children’s Services Workers.  Her involvement has been
critical in ensuring that new Society workers were able to obtain a complete
understanding of M. and her needs.   Despite the strong attachment which she
and M. have developed, she has maintained an appropriate appreciation of the
role which she has in M.’s life, and the potential that M. could have been
returned home.

[
23
]

M.B. called Society Parent Support Worker Ms.
Phillips, the grandmother and M.B.’s partner, J.C., as witnesses.  Neither the
Society nor counsel for the children raised any concerns respecting their
credibility.  I found both of them to be reliable and credible.  They presented
as fair and even handed in giving their testimony, and their evidence was not
undermined in any material way on cross examination.

[
24
]

M.B. testified at length during the trial.  I
had major concerns regarding his reliability and credibility.  As I will
discuss in further detail below, he could not recall basic information about some

He testified that he did not complete any Income

b)

As I will discuss in further detail below, M.B.
denied having received assessment reports respecting the children, despite the

He advised Society Intake Worker Ms. Ashley

f)

M.B. and V.B. both testified about an incident
that occurred on their wedding day, during which a family member became
aggressive and out of control.  Their versions of this event were completely

The Supreme Court of Canada set out the
fundamental principles that apply on a Status Review Application under the
CFSA

in
M.C.,
Supra.  It stated that in dealing with child protection
cases pursuant to the
CFSA,
the court must always keep in mind the
overall purpose and rationale of the global legislative scheme.  It held that
the underlying philosophy of the Act is that the best interests of children
must be balanced with the importance of keeping the family unit intact. The
court concluded that this philosophy is the foundational starting point for
determining the applicable test on a Status Review Application.  It emphasized
the importance of avoiding unduly restrictive interpretations of the individual
sections of the Act which may work at cross purposes with this overall
philosophy.  Applying these general principles, the court held that in a Status
Review Application, it is not necessary to retry the original need for
protection order.  As the court stated at paragraph 35 of its judgment, “that
order is set in time, and it must be assumed that it has been properly made at
that time.”  However, the court also rejected the suggestion that the test in
Status Review proceedings involves a pure best interests analysis that places
the state and parents on an equal footing with respect to the care of the
child.  Rather, it set out a two-fold test for the determination of Status
Review Applications.  The first branch of the test requires the court to
determine whether the child continues to be in need of protection, and as a
result requires a court order for their protection.  The second branch of the
test involves a consideration of the best interests of the child.

[
69
]

With respect to the first part of the test in
Status Review proceedings, the Supreme Court did not state that the child must
be found to be “in need of protection” as that phrase is defined in
section
37(2)
(b) of the
CFSA
.
What is required is that the child welfare agency
involved must justify ongoing state intervention in the life of the family by
proving that a court order continues to be necessary to protect the child in
the future.  The Ontario Court of Appeal recently reiterated this point in
Children’s
Aid Society of Oxford County v W.T.C.
,
2013 ONCA 491 (CanLII)
, 2013 CarswellOnt 10258 (C.A.). The
Supreme Court emphasized in
M.(C.)
,
that a preliminary determination of
whether ongoing state intervention is required to protect the child is
important to ensure that the overall objectives of the
CFSA
are
protected and promoted.   In support of its decision on this issue, the court
relied heavily on the fact that these statutory objectives include the
preservation of the autonomy and integrity of the family unit, and the
provision of child protection services in the least restrictive and disruptive
manner.  The court also held that the inquiry into the child’s continued need
for protection involves more than simply analyzing the events and concerns that
triggered the child welfare intervention in the first instance and determining
if those concerns persist.  Rather, the issue must be assessed from the
perspective of both the child and the parents, taking into account the reality
that the needs and circumstances of both evolve continually.  A finding that
the child continues to require protection can be  based on ongoing concerns
respecting the parents’ ability to meet the child’s needs, or for reasons
unrelated to the parties’ parenting, such as concern about the effects of
removing the child from a long-term caregiver who is able to present a
permanent plan.

“[t]he test is not whether the parents have now seen the

Aid Society of Hamilton v. A.M.,
[2012] O.J. No. 5141 (S.C.J.)
). As
Katarynych, J. stated in

“Child development

v. M.A.,
2012 ONSC 267 (CanLII)
, [2012] O.J. No. 223 (S.C.J.);
Children’s Aid Society of the
Districts of Nipissing and Parry Sound v. L.M.,
2008 ONCA 491 (CanLII)
, [2008] O.J. No. 2438 (C.A.)).

II.
Access

[
74
]

Section 58(1)
of the
CFSA

provides that
the court may, in the child’s best interests, when making an order under Part
III of the Act or upon application make, vary or terminate an order respecting
a person’s access to a child, or the child’s access to a person. The section
further provides that the court may impose such terms and conditions on any
access order which the court considers appropriate.
Section 59(2.1)
deals
specifically with the issue of access once a Crown wardship order is made.
That provision establishes a presumption against access if the child is made a Crown
ward, as follows:

Access: Crown ward

59
(2.1)
A
court shall not make or vary an access order made under section 58 with respect
to a Crown ward unless the court is satisfied that,

a)

the relationship between the person and the child is beneficial and
meaningful to the child; and

b)

the ordered access will not impair the child’s future opportunities
for adoption.

[
75
]

The presumption against access when a child is
made a Crown ward reflects the focus of the
CFSA

once Crown wardship is
ordered of maximizing the child’s opportunity to benefit from a permanent and
stable placement as part of a positive and secure family unit (
Catholic
Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v. L.S.,
2011 ONSC 5850 (CanLII)
, 2011 CarswellOnt 11097
(S.C.J.);
Children’s Aid Society of Niagara Region v. J.C.,
2007 CanLII 8919 (ON SCDC)
, 2007
CarswellOnt 1680 (Div. Ct.)). This policy is embodied in
section 63.1
of the
CFSA
,
which creates an obligation on the Society to make all reasonable efforts to
assist a child who has been made a Crown ward to develop a positive, secure and
enduring relationship within a family through either adoption, a custody order
or a plan for customary care in the case of an Indian or native child.  The
onus is on a person seeking access to a Crown ward to satisfy the court on a
balance of probabilities that both of the criteria set out in section 59(2.1)
have been satisfied (
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. M. (L.),
2011 ONCJ 146 (CanLII)
, 2011
CarswellOnt 2068 (O.C.J.);
Children’s Aid Society of Niagara Region v. J.C.,

Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v. C.G.,
Supra.)

[
76
]

With respect to the first branch of the
threshold test set out in section 59(2.1), the focus is on the importance of
the relationship from the child’s perspective, not from the perspective of the
parent seeking access (
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v.
B.(T.),
2013 CarswellOnt 14031 (S.C.J.)
;
Catholic Children’s Aid
Society of Hamilton v. L.S. (Supra)
;
Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton
v. C.H.,
[2014] O.J. No. 2921 (S.C.J.)
;
Children’s Aid Society of
Hamilton v. C.G.,
Supra.).  Quinn, J. outlined a number of important principles
relating to the test in

Children’s Aid Society
of Niagara Region v. J.(M),
2004 CanLII 2667 (ON SC)
, 2004
CarswellOnt 2800 (S.C.J.)
.
He held that a beneficial relationship is
one that is “advantageous,” and a meaningful relationship is one that is
“significant.”  He concluded that the existence of some positive aspects in the
relationship between a child and a parent is not sufficient to meet the first
part of the test in section 59(2.1); rather, it must be shown that the
relationship is significantly advantageous to the child.  (see also
Children’s
Aid Society of Niagara Region v. J.C.
,
Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society
of Hamilton v. C.G.,
Supra.)

[
77
]

Evidence indicating that a parent loves the
child, that the child loves the parent, and that some visits were pleasant will
not necessarily be sufficient to establish that the relationship is meaningful
and beneficial to the child.  This is particularly so where there is evidence
of a number of other factors and dynamics respecting the parent which have
impacted on the child’s emotional health and well-being (
Children’s Aid
Society of Niagara Region v. J.C.,
Supra., at para. 29;
Children’s Aid
Society of Toronto v. M.A.
,
2006 CanLII 1671 (ON SC)
, [2006] O.J. No. 254 (O.C.J.);
Children’s
Aid Society of Peel Region v. S. (M.),
2006 ONCJ 523 (CanLII)
, [2006] O.J. No. 5344 (O.C.J.);
Children’s
Aid Society of Hamilton v. C.H.,
Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society of
Hamilton v. C.G.,
Supra.).  The fact that access has been appropriate, with
no particular concerns noted, may also be insufficient to found a claim for
access after Crown wardship is ordered (
Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton
v. M.(W.),
2008 CanLII 53130 (ON SC)
, [2008] O.J. No. 4052 (S.C.J.);
Children’s Aid Society of
Hamilton v. C.G.,
Supra.).  Furthermore, the focus of the inquiry is the
nature and quality of the relationship between the child and the parent at the
time of trial, and not on whether it may be possible for a parent to resolve
their shortcomings so as to pave the way for a relationship that may be
meaningful and beneficial to the child in the future (
Children’s Aid Society
of Hamilton v. M.(W.),
Supra., at para. 46;
Children’s Aid Society of
Niagara Region v. D.B.,
[2011] O.J. No. 4956 (S.C.J.)
;
Children’s Aid
Society of Niagara Region v. J.C.,
Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society of
Bruce v. D.J.
2013 ONSC 717
(S.C.J.);
Catholic Children’s Aid Society
of Hamilton v. T.D. and A.A.,
2013 ONSC 5650
(S.C.J.);
Children’s Aid
Society of Hamilton v. C.H.,
Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton
v. C.G.,
Supra.).

[
78
]

With respect to the issue of whether access will
impair the child’s future opportunities for adoption, the onus of proof remains
on the parent to demonstrate the access will not result in any such
impairment.  Pazaratz, J. described this onus in
Catholic Children’s Aid
Society of Hamilton v. L.S.
, Supra., as being an onus “to satisfy the court
that access to the Crown ward will not diminish, reduce, jeopardize or
interfere with the child’s future opportunities for adoption.”   In
Catholic
Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. M. (M.)
, Supra., Sherr, J. held that
the phrase “impair the child’s future opportunity for adoption” entails more
than just impairing a child’s opportunity to
actually
be adopted.
Rather, the concept of impairment extends to concerns about undue delay in the
child being adopted.

[
79
]

Evidence indicating that a child may be
difficult to place for adoption because of their particular profile is not
sufficient to satisfy the criterion set out in
section 59(2.1)
(b) of the
CFSA

(
Children’s Aid Society of Halton Region v. M.(K.C.)
,
2012
CarswellOnt 15061 (O.C.J.)
;
Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. P.(D.),
2005 CanLII 34560 (ON CA)
, [2005]
O.J. No. 4075 (C.A.)).

There is no onus on the Society in a hearing
regarding access to a Crown ward to establish that the child is adoptable, or
to identify an actual prospective adoptive family for the child (
Children’s
Aid Society of Niagara Region v. J.C.,
Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society
of Hamilton v. A.D.L.,
Supra., at para. 159;
Children’s Aid Society of
Hamilton v. A.M.,
Supra.;
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton
v. L.S.,
Supra.;
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. M.(M.)
,
Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v. W.M.,
2008 CanLII 53130 (ON SC)
, [2008] O.J. No.
4052 (S.C.J.)).  While permanency planning through adoptive placement is one of
the long term options for Crown wards under the
CFSA,
the Society cannot
be expected to guarantee that adoption will occur or be successful in every
case.  The Society’s obligation regarding long term placement of Crown wards is
described in the legislation in more reasonable terms as an obligation to “make
all reasonable efforts to assist the child to develop a positive, secure and
enduring relationship within a family” through adoption, a custody order or a
plan for customary care in the case of Indian or native children (
CFSA,
section
63.1).

[
80
]

In the past, a Society was not able to place a Crown
ward for adoption if there was an access order in place (see former 141.1(a),
CFSA
).
As a result of this restriction, the second branch of the test for access
following a Crown wardship order was extremely difficult for parents to meet.
The
CFSA
has been amended, and
section 141.1.1(1)
now provides that Societies
may plan for the adoption of Crown wards in respect of whom there is an
outstanding access order.  If the Crown ward is in fact placed for adoption,

section 143
of the
CFSA
provides that every access order made under Part
III of the Act is terminated.  However, in these circumstances, the Society is
required to give notice to any person entitled to access of the intention to
place the child for adoption, and the person has the right to apply for an
openness order within thirty days after receiving the notice.

[
81
]

The amendments to the
CFSA

have given
parties seeking access to Crown wards a somewhat greater scope of argument in
advancing their case for access, since an access order is no longer a bar to
placing a Crown ward for adoption.    However, these changes open the door only
slightly with respect to an access claim, given that a person whose access
rights to a Crown ward have been terminated as a result of the child’s placement
for adoption may apply for continued contact to the child through an openness
order (see
CFSA
section 145.1;
Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v.
A.B.,
[2013] O.J. No. 410 (O.C.J.)
).

[
82
]

The case-law has set out the following factors
and considerations which the court should take into account in determining
whether parents have met the second branch of the test set out in
section
59(2.1)
(b) of the
CFSA
:

a)

The court should consider whether an access order could have a
chilling effect on prospective adoptive parents and decrease the pool of
possible adoptive placements, having regard for the following:

i.

there would be the spectre of a possible
openness application and protracted litigation;

ii.

the adoption process may be delayed as a result
of the litigation;

iii.

the prospective adoptive parents would not know
what form an openness order may have;

iv.

there may be concern that the child will have
difficulty fully settling and integrating into the family unit if openness were
ordered;  and

v.

if an openness order were granted, the
prospective adoptive parents would have to deal with the additional challenges
of managing contact and dealing with the parents, without the assistance of the
Society unless the Society agreed to remain involved. (
Catholic Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. M.(M.),
Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society of the
Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. M.(L.),
2013 CarswellOnt 17402
(S.C.J.)
;
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. B.(S.S.),
[2012]
O.J. No. 4160 (O.C.J.)
;
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v.
L.D.E.
,
2012 ONCJ 530 (CanLII)
, [2012] O.J. No. 4019 (O.C.J.)).

b)

Indicators that a parent will clearly be unable to support a
permanent placement for the child and will persist in attempting to have the
child returned to their care may militate against an order for access (
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. C.(L.),

[2013] O.J. No. 53 (O.C.J.)
).

c)

Evidence that parents have been able to work in a cooperative and
reasonable manner with the Society and  the child’s caregivers, including
foster parents, with respect to the needs of the child, and that they have not
undermined the child’s placement, may assist the parents in meeting the hurdle
which
section 59(2.1)
(b) places on them (
Children’s Aid Society of the
Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. M.(L.)
, Supra.;
Children’s Aid
Society of Ottawa v. F.(K.),
2013 CarswellOnt 15911 (S.C.J.)
;
Catholic
Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. L.D.E.,
Supra.;
Children’s Aid
Society of Toronto v. S.A., R.M. and S.R.,

[2012] O.J. No. 377 (O.C.J.)
;
Children’s
Aid Society of the Region of Peel v. A.R.,
[2013] O.J. No. 2969 (O.C.J.)
;
Children’s
Aid Society of the Region of Peel v. D.W.,
[2013] O.J. No. 2970 (O.C.J.)
).

d)

Conversely, evidence that parents have been unable to work with the
Society, other professionals, or the child’s caregivers in a reasonable and
respectful manner, or that they have been critical of the caregivers and made
attempts to undermine them, may cause the court to conclude that an access
order would impair the child’s adoption prospects.  The rationale for this is that
the parents’ difficult behaviour with professionals and caregivers may be a
predictor of whether the parents would be able to support an adoptive placement
with an openness order in effect (
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto
v. B.(S.S.)
, Supra.;
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v.
L.S.,
2011 ONSC 5850 (CanLII)
, [2011] O.J. No. 4512 (S.C.J.)).

e)

The nature of the protection concerns will be relevant to the
analysis required pursuant to section 59(2.1)(b).  Evidence of a history of
criminal or dangerous behaviour on the part of the access applicants may lead
the court to conclude that ongoing contact would impact negatively on the
prospects for a successful adoption, given the concerns which such a history
may pose for the security and stability of prospective adoptive parents (
Children’s
Aid Society of Halton Region v. M.(K.C.),
Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society
of Toronto v. S.A., R.M. and S.R.,
Supra.).

[
83
]

In dealing with the considerations set out
above, the court must be cautious not to engage in pure speculation regarding
the impact of an access order and a possible openness application on the
child’s prospects for adoption.  Evidence specifically addressing the relevant
considerations is required. With respect to the potential impact on the
availability of adoptive applicants, simply assuming that access will diminish
the pool of applicants is highly problematic.  As Murray, J. stated in
Catholic
Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. M.M.
, Supra., there may in fact be
many situations where the Society and/or prospective adoptive parents could
consider some form of ongoing contact between the child and the parents to be
beneficial in terms of adoptive prospects having regard for the unique
circumstances of the case.

[
84
]

The analysis of whether access should be ordered
with respect to a Crown ward does not end if the person seeking access
satisfies the criteria set out in
section 59(2.1)
of the
CFSA
.
Those
criteria constitute the threshold test that must be met in order to proceed
with the request for access.  If the threshold test is met, the court must then
determine whether the access is in the best interests of the child, and if so,
how access should be structured and any appropriate conditions of access, taking
into consideration all of the factors set out in
section 37(3)
of the
CFSA
(
Children’s
Aid Society of Niagara Region v. J.(M),
Supra.;
Children’s Aid Society
of the Niagara Region v. J.C.
,
Supra.).

[
85
]

The principles outlined above relate to requests
by parents or other adult persons for access to Crown wards.  In this case,
there is also a request for an order for sibling access.  Different legal
principles apply under the
CFSA

to sibling access as opposed to a
request for access by a parent or another adult.  The test for determining
whether a sibling access order should be made with respect to a Crown ward is
the best interests of the child (
Children’s Aid Society of Niagara Region v.
J.C.,
Supra., at para. 26).

PART V:  ANALYSIS

I.
ISSUE
# 1:  ARE THE CHILDREN STILL IN NEED OF PROTECTION?

A.
Overview

[
86
]

The first issue to determine in this case is whether
the children continue to require protection through court intervention.  I am
satisfied based on the extensive evidence adduced at trial that the subject
children continue to be in need of protection.  There is a longstanding history
of numerous protection concerns in this case dating from 1999.  The protection
concerns have been serious and persistent since that time, and include the
following:

a)

Horrific home conditions;

b)

Concerns regarding physical neglect;

c)

Concerns regarding physical harm to the children and risk of
physical harm due to poor judgment and inadequate supervision of the children;

d)

Educational neglect;

e)

Concerns
regarding sexual abuse or exposure to extremely inappropriate sexual activities
or programming;

f)

Concerns regarding the father M.B.’s emotional volatility and
aggression;

g)

The
father’s physical and emotional limitations;

h)

The
unstable lifestyle of V.B. and M.B.;

i)

The father’s limited involvement in caring for the children and in supporting
V.B. in meeting the children’s needs;

j)

The father’s knowledge of the protection concerns respecting V.B., and
the inability of both parents to appreciate the seriousness of the concerns;

k)

The
father’s failure to present a plan for the children in a timely manner;

l)

The parents’ inability to prioritize the children’s needs and best
interests;  and

m)

Significant
cognitive and psychological limitations on the part of both V.B. and M.B. which
have impacted on their parenting capacity.

[
87
]

I review each of these areas of concern in detail below.

B.
Concerns Respecting the
Conditions of the Family Home

[
88
]

One of the most persistent and significant
problems throughout the CCAS’s and the Society’s involvement with this family
has been the unsanitary and unsafe conditions of the family home.  This was a
major area of concern both prior to and after the parties separated.  During
the intervention that spanned from February 23, 2006
until January 2, 2008, the CCAS verified serious concerns regarding the
presence of safety hazards, general unsanitary conditions and major clutter
that posed a risk for young children.  As I have already noted, in May 2007,
the home environment became so unsafe and unhygienic that the CCAS directed the
mother to leave the home with the children for a two week period to allow the
father to de-clutter, clean and repair it.  Of particular concern at that time
was the kitchen, where there was a large hole in the ceiling that M.B. had
simply covered with a tarp.  Similar issues presented during the CCAS
intervention from March 2008 until January 2009.   I find that during that
time, CCAS staff identified ongoing problems about various safety hazards in
the home, including cigarette butts that were within reach of the young
children, exposed wires that posed a risk of tripping, and stairways that were
not blocked off with safety gates.

[
89
]

As previously noted in these Reasons, the
current intervention with this family began as a result of a report from a
plumber with concerns about the state of the mother’s home.  The plumber had been
at the home located at W[…] Street in Hamilton on August 31, 2010 to carry out repairs.
Society workers Ms. Madeline Kingdon and Ms. Leianne Cockerill attended the
home on that date and determined that the home conditions were so deplorable
that the children had to be removed immediately from the residence.  They made
arrangements for V.B. and the children to stay with an aunt for the night.  V.B.
and the children subsequently relocated to the Good Shepherd shelter.  Society
worker Kim Colangelo attended the home the next day.  The father M.B. was there
to let her into the home.  Ms. Colangelo testified at trial that the conditions
of the mother’s home on this date were the worst home conditions that she had
ever seen throughout her career as a social worker.  Ms. Colangelo and Ms.
Kingdon took photographs of the home, which were marked as Exhibit 6 at trial.
The photographs depict a horrific state of affairs in the home.  Based on these
photographs and the evidence of Ms. Colangelo, I make the following findings
regarding the home conditions:

a)

The house was completely cluttered with various
items and debris.  A number of the rooms were inaccessible due to the clutter,
and the entrance to the home was largely blocked by various items.

b)

There were no sheets on any of the beds, with
the exception of one top sheet on the master bedroom bed, and the mattresses
were filthy.

c)

There was only one crib that was located in the
master bedroom, and which was full of items.  It could not be used for a child
to sleep in.

d)

There was a hole in the ceiling in the kitchen,
and the only source of running water was the tap in the upstairs bathroom.

e)

There were garbage bags and piles of dirty baby
diapers located throughout the house.

f)

The sinks in the home were full of stagnant
water, and many flies were present throughout the residence.  There were strips
of fly tape hanging throughout the house, and the strips were completely
covered with dead flies.

g)

There were dirty dishes and rotting food throughout
the kitchen, and one of the dishes in the sink was full of maggots.   There
were also plates with food on them in the living room, and rotting food and
take-out containers in the master bedroom.

h)

The kitchen counters, the stove and the floors were
utterly filthy.

i)

There was a container in the kitchen that
appeared to have caught fire.

j)

There appeared to be mould on the ceiling in one
of the bedrooms.

k)

One of the walls in the master bedroom was badly
damaged and duct-taped.

l)

The roof over the porch off the kitchen area was
falling down and was held up by the screen door.

m)

There were wires hanging from the ceiling.

n)

Clothes were strewn throughout the house and all
over the furniture.

o)

There was an extremely foul odour throughout the
home.

p)

The outside yard and side of the home were
cluttered with junk and garbage.

q)

There were very few items of food in the fridge,
and there was a strong odour of rotting food.

r)

All of the garbage, clutter, debris and rotting
food were within reach of the children.

s)

There were no baby gates installed in the home,
despite the fact that A. was only 10 months old at the time.

[
90
]

I find that the state of the home in September
2010 was so deplorable that it posed a major safety and health risk for the
children.  Ms. Colangelo was so concerned for the well-being of the children
after observing the home that she referred the children for an assessment by
the Child Advocacy and Assessment Program (“CAAP) partly to determine whether
their physical health had been jeopardized from exposure to toxins and mould.
Ms. Colangelo also arranged for the Salvation Army to attend the home to remove
some of the furniture and put it in storage so that the property manager for
the residence could attend and assess the situation.  However, when the
Salvation Army staff attended the home, they refused to take the items in
question because they were so filthy.

[
91
]

The concerns regarding the mother’s ability to
maintain appropriate home conditions persisted during her stay at the shelter
with the children from September until December 2010.  During that time period,
shelter and CCAS staff noted that V.B.’s apartment was often in general
disarray, that V.B. was unable to stay on top of laundry, that clothing and
bedding were at times shoved into the closet such that they fell out when the
closet was opened and that there was often very little food in the
refrigerator.

[
92
]

The mother’s home conditions continued to be
very problematic when the mother secured her new residence in December 2010.
For a period of time, the subject children and their brother M.B. Jr. all
shared two mattresses in one bedroom because the parents had not obtained
appropriate bedding for them.  When Ms. Abell attended the home on March 15,
2011, the parents had still not obtained appropriate mattresses and beds.  On
that date, Ms. Abell found the home to be filthy and hazardous.  The house was
cluttered, there were numerous garbage bags in the corner of the kitchen, the
stove was filthy and there was a package of cigarettes on the floor within
reach of the children.  When Ms. Abell attended the home on April 27, 2011 to
discuss the CCAS’s plan to apprehend N.B. and S.B., she again found the home to
be filthy, smelly and extremely cluttered, with dirty clothing strewn
throughout the house.

[
93
]

As I have already noted, the CCAS’s decision to
apprehend the children from the mother’s care on August 16, 2011 was prompted
in part by the deplorable conditions of the mother’s home at that time.  I find
that when CCAS workers Ms. Abell and Ms. Nguyen attended the home on that date,
the home was again in a state that was unfit and hazardous for the children.
Photographs of the home which Ms. Abell and Ms. Nguyen took on this date were
marked as Exhibit 16 at trial.  The concerns regarding the home included the
following:

a)

The kitchen was extremely dirty and unhygienic.
There were dirty dishes piled up on the counter and the sink, and dirty pots on
the stove.

b)

The refrigerator was filthy and covered in mould
and contained no food.  The mother later insisted that there was another
refrigerator in the home that contained food, but she never disclosed this or
showed the other refrigerator to CCAS staff at the time.  There were only a few
canned goods in the kitchen cabinets.

c)

There were dirty clothes and dirty diapers lying
around the house, including on shelves and tables.

d)

There was a fan in operation in the living room
that had no cover, such that the blades were exposed and posed a hazard for the
children.

e)

There was broken glass and garbage all over the
floor in the upstairs room.

f)

The washrooms were filthy, and there were dirty
plates covered with old food throughout the home which were attracting flies.

[
94
]

Concerns regarding the mother’s home conditions
continued after the children were apprehended in August 2011, and were a
significant factor in the Society’s decision to apprehend the children again on
April 4, 2014.   In September 2013, the child S. reported to his foster mother
that there was a large amount of dog feces in the girls’ room during a visit at
the mother’s home, and that there were many flies around the feces.  On
February 9, 2014, the child M. reported to her foster mother that the cats and
dogs in the mother’s home had urinated and defecated on the children’s beds.
Society Children’s Services worker Tory Baker-Reed attended the mother’s home
on February 25, 2014, and observed dishes with rotting food all over the home, heaps
of rotting compost on the kitchen counter, clothes strewn throughout the
residence, general clutter and no sheets on the beds.  The home smelled of
rotting food, cigarette smoke and animal urine, and Ms. Baker-Reed noted that
the basement door was blocked with bags of garbage and dirty clothing.   V.B.
reported to Ms. Baker-Reed on that date that the dog had defecated and urinated
on the sheets.  The child S. stated at that time that it was not a problem that
the animals defecated on the mattresses because when this happened, they simply
flipped the mattresses over.  On April 22, 2014, the child S. reported to
Children’s Services Worker Ms. Conley that the mother’s home was a disaster.
He described seeing rats climbing over his sweaters in his bedroom closet, and explained
in detail how he had tried to catch a rat in the kitchen with a small cage.
The child M. disclosed similar concerns regarding the mother’s home at that
time.

[
95
]

V.B. acknowledged at trial that the conditions
of her home were often unacceptable.  With respect to the concerns in August
2010, she advised Ms. Abell that she was upset about her separation from the
father and that this had affected her ability to maintain the home.  However,
the parents’ physical separation had occurred a year earlier, and V.B.
testified at trial that their relationship in fact continued until April 2013.
V.B.’s explanation for the poor home conditions on August 16, 2011 was that she
had attended for a tubal ligation at the hospital that day and had not had

II.
ISSUE #2:  WHAT PLACEMENT IS IN THE
BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN?

Overview

basis as set out in
section 70
of the
CFSA

members of the community have come forward to present a plan for the children.

in this case, including those specifically enumerated in
section 37(3)
of the
CFSA,
