how much he enjoys visits with his father.  When his access with M.B. was
increased, he began to talk about wanting to live with his father.

G
.
The
Children’s Needs

[
189
]

The children have all been in care far beyond the statutorily mandated
time limits set out in the
CFSA
.,
and they have all been subjected to
significant trauma due to their experiences while in the care of their
parents.  The primary needs of all five children at this point are for
certainty and stability with respect to their long-term living situations and
their relationships with the important people in their lives.  They have all
remained in limbo far too long.  All of them have suffered emotionally due to
the tremendous uncertainty in their lives resulting from two apprehensions,
changes in access arrangements with their parents, attempts at reintegration
and changes in foster placements.  All of the children have shown signs of
stress due to this uncertainty around their placement and access.   In this
regard, I find as follows:

a)

The
child M. has demonstrated anxiety after visits, both at school and in the
foster home.  She would often become verbally and physically aggressive, clingy
and defiant, and would complain about somatic illnesses at school following
visits.  She exhibited extremely concerning signs of distress during the period
leading up to the planned date for her return to the care of her mother in
December 2013.  As visits in the mother’s home moved to overnights and were
extended, her behaviours upon her return to the foster home became more
extreme.   She began to have major rages, was terrified at night, took hours to
settle at bed time and had frequent nightmares.  When visits with V.B. returned
to the Society access centre following the second apprehension in April 2014, M.’s
behaviours improved and her nightmares ceased.  However, when visits with the
mother began at the home of the paternal grandmother in September 2014, M.’s
behaviours became problematic once again.  She became extremely defiant, oppositional
and verbally and physically aggressive with her foster mother.  On October 13,
2014, she drew three pictures and put them on the stairs for her foster
mother.  The first picture said “sad” and the second one was of a sad face.
The third picture was of a decapitated head with two hands reaching for the
face.  That same night, M. had a complete emotional breakdown, wanted to talk
about memories and said that she wanted to stay with her foster mother forever,
but that she was scared to talk about her wishes for fear of upsetting her
parents.

b)

The
children Sh. and V. Jr. have also experienced anxiety around changes in their
visits.  During the children’s reintegration into the mother’s care, Sh. became
extremely teary, unsettled and clingy with her foster mother.   As the return
date got closer, her anxiety increased and she began to talk about missing her
foster family  When the mother’s visits began at the home of the paternal
grandmother in the fall of 2014, Sh. became oppositional, upset and began yelling
a great deal.  She developed an irrational fear of spiders, had great
difficulty falling asleep and became obsessed about knowing the precise plan
for the following day.  During this same period, V. Jr. began to make regular
complaints about not feeling well.

c)

A.
has also shown signs of being unsettled when access arrangements have changed.
He demonstrated increased aggression when he was being reintegrated into V.B.’s
care starting in the summer of 2013.  Although A. indicated that he enjoyed his
increased access with his father in 2014, school staff reported that they
noticed a marked increase in his challenging behaviours at school following
visits with M.B., including his general non-compliance, running, hiding from
teachers, sneaking snacks and not following directions.

[
190
]

Each of the children has particular characteristics and needs that must
be considered in deciding their best interests.  Dealing first with the eldest
of the subject children S., as I have already discussed, he has highly inappropriate
knowledge of sexual matters for his age and has a history of engaging in
inappropriate sexual behaviours with other children.  He requires long-term
counselling to address these issues.  This treatment has been put on hold until
a decision is made regarding his placement and access.  S. suffers from Attention
Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and requires medication on a consistent
basis to address his symptoms.  If he does not receive his medication, his
behaviours become extremely difficult and he has problems regulating his
emotions.  Even when he is on his medication, he has difficulty interacting
appropriately with others.  He tends to invade people’s space, can be pushy at
times and has to be told to bathe.  He can be somewhat scattered, struggles to
stay organized and has problems following directions that involve more than one
or two steps.  S. is otherwise a healthy child.  Academically, S. has just completed grade 4.  He has difficulties at times
focussing in the classroom.  S. struggles with Language and Math and is on an
Individual Education Plan in relation to those subjects.  His reading skills
are delayed, and his foster mother has to give him extra help and support with
reading on a daily basis in order for him to stay on course.

[
191
]

Despite S.’s many challenges, he is an extremely loving
child who cares deeply about others.  He has developed a strong attachment to
his current foster family, and all indicators are that this could be a long
term placement if he remains in care.  S. requires a highly competent
caregiver who is able to consistently and diligently monitor him with other
children, administer his medication for his ADHD, ensure his attendance at counselling
and school, provide him with emotional nurturance and meet his basic physical
needs.  It is of the utmost importance for him to live in an environment where
there is a great deal of structure and a predictable routine.

[
192
]

The child M. has many special needs.  I have already described her
extremely inappropriate knowledge of sexual matters and her sexually
provocative and aggressive behaviours.  Like S., she desperately requires
long-term counselling to deal with these issues.  Her treatment through Child
and Adolescent Services relating to her sexual behaviours has been put on hold
until a permanent decision is made about her future.  This treatment must
resume as soon as possible so that M. can begin to work through the traumatic
events that caused these behaviours to emerge.  M. also has periods when she
suffers from severe anxiety and rages.   As discussed above, her anxiety levels
increased during periods of access changes.  Her foster mother reports that she
needs a great deal of structure in her day to day life and a consistent
routine.  She needs to know the plans for the next day, but if she is told the
plan too far ahead she becomes stressed.  If her foster mother becomes upset
with her, she panics and has an emotional meltdown.   Accordingly, it is
important for her caregiver to process frustration internally first and then
respond in a calm way to her.  Unfortunately, M. has great difficulty opening
up about her feelings and issues of concern to her.  She will likely continue
to have difficulties in this regard until she knows that she is in a safe,
stable and permanent placement.

[
193
]

M. has had issues with her weight for a number of years, and her food
intake must be carefully monitored to ensure that she does not become obese.  When
she first came into care, she engaged in gorging and food hoarding behaviours.
These problems have improved over time.  There have been occasions when she has
made herself vomit after eating too much, and she needs to be carefully
monitored to ensure that she does not develop an eating disorder.  M. also has
issues with bedwetting, especially during times when she is feeling stressed.  She
is active and her foster mother has involved her in many activities.   M. is
experiencing some challenges at school.  Her reading and writing are delayed,
and she has problems focusing at times.

[
194
]

M. requires a caregiver who is extremely patient, and who is able to
diligently and consistently monitor her interactions with other children,
ensure her attendance at school and treatment, provide her with emotional
security and nurturance and meet her basic physical needs.  Her caregiver must
be trained and effective in managing and responding to sexualized and
aggressive behaviours and extreme anxiety.  Her foster mother testified that
she could not imagine being able to parent another child along with M. due to
her extremely high needs.  M. has suffered a great deal in her short life and
cannot tolerate any further uncertainty or upheaval of any sort.   Her foster
mother has received training about how to manage and respond to sexualized
behaviours, healthy attachment building and therapeutic parenting.  She is
willing to care for M. on a long term basis.

[
195
]

Sh. is doing very well in foster care.  She is a high energy
child and is generally in good health.  However, her behaviours are challenging
at times.  As I have already indicated, she has exhibited sexualized conduct and
has been involved in inappropriate sexual activity with her siblings.  She often
presents as emotionally needy and attention-seeking, and seeks frequent recognition
and reassurance from her foster mother.  When society workers
come to the home, she clambers for their attention.  She sometimes lacks
discrimination regarding the people who she should approach.

[
196
]

Sh. continues to exhibit significant signs of
anxiety.  She insists on knowing the schedule for the day, and can become
extremely upset if events do not unfold as she wishes them to.  She has temper
tantrums if she does not get her own way, and she can be bossy and pushy.  Despite
Sh.’s numerous challenges, she is described as a sweet child who wears her
heart on her sleeve.  She is very intelligent and well liked among her peers,
and she is not experiencing any difficulties or delays in school.

[
197
]

V. Jr. is a healthy child who is doing well in
foster care.  However, she also exhibits needy and attention-seeking behaviours
in the foster home, and has been involved in inappropriate sexual activities
with her siblings.  She is more cautious and introverted than her sister Sh.
and needs encouragement to try new things.  The Society had a consultation with
developmental pediatrician Dr. Benjamin Klein respecting V. Jr. on November 24,
2014.  The Society’s concerns respecting V. Jr. as of that time included
academic delays, difficulties carrying out multi-step commands, forgetfulness
and the need for constant redirection.  However, V. Jr. presented as socially
appropriate and there were no concerns regarding her gross or fine motor
development.  Dr. Klein concluded that V. Jr.’s knowledge of sexuality was
beyond age appropriate knowledge expectations, and was suggestive of sexual
abuse and/or inappropriate exposure to adult sexuality.  He also concluded that
her history was suggestive of a learning disability, possibly cognitive delays
and executive functioning deficits.  He recommended that reading interventions
for V. Jr. begin right away.  Based on these conclusions, the Society has
arranged for V. Jr. to undergo a comprehensive developmental assessment by Dr.
Klein.

[
198
]

The Society made a referral for Sh. and V. Jr.
to receive services from the Intensive Child and Family Services program due to
their many special needs.  The children began to receive services from this
program in January 2015.  In addition, because of their high needs and the
necessity for constant supervision, their foster family receives a special rate
as well as the right to receive respite relief one weekend each month.  To
date, the foster parents have not availed themselves of the respite care that
has been offered to them.

[
199
]

A. is a healthy and active child.  In 2012, concerns were noted
regarding his impulsivity, his tendency to bolt when under stress or in public,
his destructive behaviours and his ability to process verbal information.  The
Society had a consultation with Dr. Klein about A. on March 21, 2013, and Dr.
Klein concluded that the information available about A. as of that time was
suggestive of possible developmental delays in language and social emotional
domains.  He recommended that A. be referred to the Chedoke Developmental
Pediatrics and Rehabilitation Program for assessment. However, the wait list
for this program was two years.  Accordingly, the Society held a further
consultation with Dr. Klein on October 21, 2014.  At that time, A. was noted to
be functioning quite well in the foster home.  In particular, he was able to
remain calm and quiet, listen to instructions and complete goals.  However, A.
was demonstrating many challenges in the school setting, including academic
delay, aggression, lack of focus, non-compliance with directions, bolting and
running from the classroom.  Dr. Klein concluded that the discrepancies between
A.’s presentation at school as opposed to the foster home was suggestive that
he did not suffer from ADHD, and recommended that he carry out a comprehensive
developmental assessment.

[
200
]

Dr. Klein completed his developmental assessment of A. in November
2014.  As of that time, A. presented as very affectionate, happy, empathetic
and eager to please in his foster home.   His foster mother was not observing
any problematic behaviours at home.  His gross motor skills were assessed as
appropriate.  However, at school, A. continued to exhibit numerous difficulties.
He was attention-seeking, had problems following all routines, directions and
instructions, was generally non-compliant, talked excessively in class,
interrupted teachers repeatedly, was easily distracted by external stimuli,
often bolted from his seat and would hide when upset or if he felt that he had
done something wrong.  Dr. Klein concluded that A. suffers from learning
disorders in Math and Reading.  In addition, he diagnosed A. as having a
neurodevelopmental disorder associated with exposure to complex trauma.  He
explained that this disorder involves deficits in self-regulation that lead to
symptoms of agitation and unregulated activity levels when environmental stress
exceeds A.’s ability to self-regulate.  This disorder is a brain-based deficit
associated with child maltreatment occurring most typically between the ages of
0 to 3 years of age.  Dr. Klein elaborated that A.’s clinical picture was
suggestive of an “insecure avoidant” or “A type attachment strategy,” in which
the child is often overly compliant in suppressing negative affect and
behaviour, but then becomes easily emotionally overwhelmed in stressful
situations.  He ruled out ADHD, partly on the basis that A.’s symptoms do not
persist across different environments.  Dr. Klein explained that the main
treatment for this disorder is to decrease the environmental stress that A. is
exposed to and to teach him emotional stress regulation skills.  His
recommendations for management of A.’s symptoms included the following:

a)

Recognize
that his behaviours are not due to wilful disobedience.

b)

Expectations
and strategies need to be modified and supported compared to other same age peers.

c)

Maintain
a calm and collaborative manner with A., including warm facial expressions,
soft voice, smiling, not a punitive or non-approving approach.

d)

Avoid
negativity or hostility, as these will trigger involuntary escalation of behaviour
such as bolting.

e)

Maintain
consistent routines and rules, with gentle cues and forewarnings.

f)

Use one-on-one or small group learning as much as possible.

g)

Avoid
noisy, chaotic environments, since A. is extremely sensitive to stress levels.

h)

Avoid
the use of the word “no,” and instead use choices, distractions and praise.

[
201
]

Dr. Klein consulted with the Society respecting A. again on November 24,
2014.  As of that time, there were ongoing concerns in the school setting about
A. bolting, having difficulties with transitions, and hiding when under
stress.  Dr. Klein reiterated that A.’s “fight or flight” behaviours are his
coping mechanisms for emotional stressors.  He provided very specific
instructions for his caregiver and school officials to follow when A.
experiences tantrums or bolts and tries to escape from his environment.

[
202
]

Based on the foregoing evidence, I find that A. requires a highly
experienced and competent caregiver who is able to provide a stable, structured
and calm environment for him where there are predictable routines.  His
caregiver needs to be extremely patient and able to comprehend and carry out
the many recommendations which Dr. Klein has made for dealing with A.   In
addition, he requires parent figures who are able to advocate for his many
needs, ensure that he receives ongoing appropriate assessment and treatment,
and meet his basic physical and emotional needs.   His caregivers must be able
to consistently provide him with the in-home support which he will require in
order to progress appropriately. A.’s current foster mother is a very
experienced and highly competent caregiver who is able to meet A.’s many
needs.  She approaches A. in a calm manner and sets clear expectations,
boundaries and routines for him.  A. does very well in this setting, and there
are no significant concerns regarding his behaviours in the home.  He has
formed positive attachments to the members of his foster family.

H.
The
Ability of the Parents to Meet the Children’s Needs

[
203
]

Based on all of my findings set out above, I conclude that neither V.B.
nor M.B. is able to meet any of the children’s needs.  M.B. has presented an
alternative position that at least the child A. should be placed in his care.
I am not satisfied that M.B. has the parenting skills to parent even one child
alone, including the child A.

[
204
]

V.B. consented to an order for Crown wardship respecting the children.
Her counsel advised that V.B. acknowledged that she was unlikely to succeed in
having the children returned to her care based on the evidence in this case.  I
am satisfied that although V.B. loves her children very much, she is simply
unable to meet their needs.  The protection concerns respecting her that I have
outlined in great detail in these Reasons are serious, long-standing in nature
and unlikely to improve over time.  The children would be at high risk of
suffering serious physical, emotional and sexual harm, as well as major neglect
of their basic needs if all or some of them were returned to V. B.’s care.

[
205
]

With respect to M.B., the protection concerns respecting him which I
have outlined in great detail are similarly very serious and long-standing in
nature.  It is concerning that he does not acknowledge responsibility for any
of the problems that led to the protracted child protection history with his
family.  He has consistently placed the entire blame for this history of child
welfare intervention on others, including V.B.  He lacks insight into the
seriousness of the concerns and the immensity of the task that he wishes to
take on of caring for all five children.  He lacks the cognitive and
psychological functioning required to effectively carry out the day to day
parenting of any of the children.  Although visits in his home proceeded
without any major incidents, the skills required for short term access periods
are very different than those involved in parenting the children on a full time
basis.  The evidence respecting M.B.’s parenting history and general lifestyle
clearly supports a finding that he is simply unable to provide any of these high
needs children with the stability, predictability, structure, emotional
nurturance, and regular attention to all of their needs which they desperately
require at this point on their lives.

III.
ISSUE #3:  SHOULD THE PARENTS BE
GRANTED ACCESS RIGHTS TO THE CHILDREN, AND IF SO WHAT TERMS OF ACCESS WOULD BE
IN THE CHILDREN’S BEST INTERESTS

[
206
]

I turn to the issue of access between the parents and the children.  The
onus is on V.B. and M.B. to establish on a balance of probabilities that their relationship with the children is meaningful and beneficial to the
children, and that any access ordered will not impair the children’s future
opportunities for adoption.   Dealing first with V.B., I am satisfied that her
relationship with the children is meaningful and beneficial to the children.
V.B. was the children’s primary caregiver throughout most of their lives.  Many
of her shortcomings as a parent related to her being completely overwhelmed in
attempting to meet the needs of so many children, with very little support from
M.B.  Despite the numerous and persistent concerns regarding her care and
supervision of the children over the years, it is clear that she loves all of
her children dearly, and that the children are very attached to her. I am
satisfied that the children would suffer significant emotional harm if their
contact with her terminated.

[
207
]

I am also satisfied that the relationship between the children and M.B.
is meaningful and beneficial to the children.  Despite the many concerns
respecting M.B. and his failure to support V.B. in the day to day struggles of
meeting the children’s needs, he has been a consistent presence in the
children’s lives.  I accept the evidence that after he left the family home in
the summer of 2009, he continued to typically see the children on a daily
basis.  I find that the children very much looked forward to their visits from
their father and enjoyed their time with him.  M.B. took them on many outings,
and I find that his visits were often the highlight of the children’s days.
M.B. maintained consistent contact with the children when they were in foster
care.  He advocated for a progression of visits to the home of his mother and
then to his own home.  Although there were concerns respecting those home
visits, as described earlier in these Reasons, the children also had many
positive reports about the visits and enjoyed the outings which M.B. took them
on.   After carefully reviewing all of the evidence, I conclude that the
children would suffer emotional harm if their relationship with their father
were to terminate altogether.

[
208
]

With respect to the second branch of the test for access, I find that an
order granting V.B. and M.B. access to the children will not impair the
children’s future opportunities for adoption.  The amendments to the
CFSA

allowing
for adoption placement despite the existence of an access order will allow the
Society to pursue adoption planning for the children while access is ongoing.  In
my view, terminating the children’s relationships with their parents at this
point would be extremely unsettling for them and could lead to emotional
difficulties which could hamper adoption planning efforts.  The children have
been through incredible turmoil and many drastic changes in their short lives,
and I find that they simply cannot cope with any more major upheaval at this
point.   The unique circumstances of this case are such that ongoing access is
more supportive of adoptive planning than no access, provided that the access
is structured appropriately.

[
209
]

The real question respecting access in this case is how access should be
structured so as to support and further the children’s best interests.  With
respect to V.B., the Minutes of Settlement which the Society, V.B. and counsel
for the children executed provide for access at minimum twice per month, and
give the Society discretion regarding the specifics of access.  This discretion
extends to whether access should be supervised, and if so, who the supervisor
should be.  The Minutes of Settlement specifically contemplate that the
grandmother may be approved as a supervisor.  The Society’s proposal for access
to M.B. is that it be in the discretion of the Society and supervised in its
discretion.  Family Services Worker Ms. Hall testified that the Society may at
some point be willing to exercise its discretion so as to allow for
unsupervised visits in the community or in the father’s home.

[
210
]

I am not satisfied that the Society’s access proposals are in the best
interests of the children.   I conclude that access to V.B. and M.B. should be
at least once per month, but no more than twice per month.  Furthermore, I have
determined that all access to both V.B. and M.B. should be supervised only by
the Society.  My decision respecting the structure and specifics of access has
been informed by the following considerations:

a)

The
children’s primary need at this time is for stability, security and
predictability.  A consistent and predictable access arrangement is in their
best interests.  While visits with their parents are in their best interests,
the visits should be limited in number so that their routines, schooling and
activities are not unduly disrupted.   The access that I am ordering will
result in the children having to be transported for access purposes up to four
times each month.  Any further disruption to the children’s schedules to
facilitate access is not in their best interests.

b)

As I
have discussed in these Reasons, the children have in the past not responded
well when access changes have occurred, and in particular, when home visits and
unsupervised access have been arranged.

c)

I
have taken into consideration the ability of the parents to support the
children’s foster placements.  I find that both V.B. and M.B. have had
difficulty supporting many of the children’s placements, and that this has had
a disruptive effect on the placements and the children.  The parents’ numerous
complaints regarding the foster parents have contributed to my decision
regarding the frequency of access.  Access must be structured in such a way as
to balance the interest on the part of the children in maintaining their
relationships with their parents with their need for a stable home setting
where they feel secure about their future.  The parents’ approach to the
children’s foster parents in the past has created a dark cloud over the
children’s placements.  As I have already discussed, V.B. and M.B. forced
changes to the children’s placements when they insisted that the child
protection file be transferred from the CCAS to the Society.  There have been
numerous complaints about the children’s foster parents since that time, none
of which have been verified after the Society investigated them.  By way of
examples, the parents raised concern that A.’s original foster parents had
physically abused him.  They have both alleged that M.’s foster mother has
influenced M. against them and that she is the cause of the child’s troubled
sexual behaviours, physical aggression and anxiety.   They made a complaint
that C.G. was physically abusive to M.  C.G. testified that after one visit
with her parents, M. returned to the foster home and said that foster families
are “fake families,” and that C.G. would get another foster daughter who she
would love more once M. was returned home.  M. has a very clear impression that
her parents do not like her foster mother.  After one visit with her mother, M.
said to C.G. “this is how much Mom hates you,” and held her arms wide apart.
Later that day, she said tearfully that she wished her parents would get along
with her foster mother.  Despite the incredible commitment and devotion which
C.G. has shown to M., the parents have repeatedly asked that M. be moved from
her care.  They stated that M.B. Jr.’s foster mother gave him cigarettes and
allowed her foster children to smoke marijuana.  The parents have also made
persistent complaints about A.’s clothes and boots being the wrong size,
despite the Society’s explanation that A. was driven straight from school to
the visits and often took other classmates’ belongings by mistake.

d)

Although
M.B. has had additional access with A. in the past, it is not in the best
interests of either A. or the other children that this special, additional
access resume.  A. has many special needs and requires as much predictability,
security and stability as possible.  While no incidents of concern occurred
during M.B.’s special visits with A., I am not satisfied that this would
continue to be the case if unsupervised home visits with A. were to resume.
M.B.’s extensive history of conflict with V.B. and various members of the
community and his poor parenting record lead me to conclude that unsupervised
home visits with M.B. would place A. at serious risk of suffering harm, neglect
and exposure to adult conflict.   Moreover, I have grave concerns regarding the
emotional impact on the other children of M.B. having special access with only
one child.

e)

The
seriousness and magnitude of the protection concerns in this case, and the
parents’ inability to acknowledge the concerns, are such that unsupervised
access is not appropriate.

f)

The evidence does not support an order allowing supervision of access to
be carried out by anyone other than Society representatives.  As I have
reviewed in detail in these Reasons, the parents have ignored the Society’s
directions regarding the parameters and conditions of their access on numerous
occasions.  The grandmother was a designated access supervisor, and she also
blatantly ignored fundamental directions which the Society established for
access.  V.B. and M.B. had many chances to prove that they could work
cooperatively with the Society so that their access could be increased and
liberalized.  Their disregard for the Society’s directions regarding access
breached any sense of trust that developed between them and the Society.  The
consequence of this breach of trust is that their access must now be supervised
only by the Society.

[
211
]

All parties and counsel for the children agree that it is in the best
interests of the children that they have access to each other and to their
other siblings, N.B. and S.B.  Having regard for the concerns about sexualized
and aggressive behaviours between the children, I conclude that all sibling
access must be supervised.

IV.
TERMS OF ORDER TO ISSUE

[
212
]

Based on the foregoing, a final order shall issue as follows:

a)

The children S., M., Sh., V. Jr. and A. (“the children”) shall be Crown wards
and shall remain in the care of the Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton (“the
Society”).

b)

The Respondents V.B. an M.B. shall have access to each of the children
at least once per month, but no more than twice per month, supervised by the
Society. The Society shall have the discretion to determine all other specifics
respecting this access.

c)

The Society shall ensure that the children have access with each other
at least twice per month, and with their other siblings, S.B. and N.B., at
least once per month.  This access shall be supervised by the Society or any
other person approved in advance by the Society.  The Society shall attempt to
arrange these visits so that they coincide as much as possible with visits
between the children and the Respondents M.B. and V.B.  The Society shall have
the discretion to determine all other specifics regarding this access.
